A '''complex number''' is the sum of a [[real number]] with an [[imaginary number]].

== Formal definition ==

$$
a+bi,\, a,b \in \mathbb{R}
$$

is a '''complex number''', where $i$ is the [[imaginary number#Formal_definition|imaginary unit]].

The set of all complex numbers can be denoted by $\mathbb{C}$.

== Complex plane ==

See [[complex plane]].

== Polar form ==

All complex numbers $z=a+bi$ can be written in polar form $r\operatorname{cis}(\theta)$, where

$$
\operatorname{cis}(\theta)=\cos\theta+i\sin\theta \\
a=r\cos\theta \\
b=r\sin\theta
$$

It can therefore be inferred:

$$
r=\sqrt{a^2+b^2} \\
\theta=
\begin{cases}
\arctan(\frac{b}{a}),\, a>0 \\
\arctan(\frac{b}{a})+\pi,\, a<0 \\
\frac{\pi}{2},\, a=0,b>0 \\
-\frac{\pi}{2},\, a=0,b<0
\end{cases}
$$

$r$ is also known as the '''modulus''' of $z$, denoted by $\left\| z \right\|$, and $\theta$ the argument of $z$, denoted by $\arg(z)$.
<ref>{{#cite:Q2335}}</ref>

=== Inverse, multiplication, division, and nth root in polar form ===

If $z=r_1\operatorname{cis}(\theta_1),\, w=r_2\operatorname{cis}(\theta_2)$, then:

$$
z^{-1}= \frac{1}{r_1} \operatorname{cis}\left({-\theta_1}\right) = \frac{1}{r_1} \cos \theta_1 - \frac{1}{r_1} i\sin \theta_1 \tag{1}\\
zw = r_1 r_2 \operatorname{cis}\left({\theta_1 + \theta_2}\right), \tag{2} \\
\frac{z}{w} = \frac{r_1}{r_2} \operatorname{cis}\left({\theta_1 - \theta_2}\right). \tag{3} \\
z^{\frac{1}{n}}=r_1^{\frac{1}{n}}\operatorname{cis}\left(\frac{\theta_1}{n}\right) \tag{4}
$$

<ref>{{#cite:Q2335}}</ref>
{{Hidden proof}}
'''Proof.'''

For (1), multiply the numerator and the denominator by $\cos\theta_1-i\sin\theta_1$:

$$
\frac{1}{\cos\theta_1+i\sin\theta_1}=\frac{\cos\theta_1-i\sin\theta_1}{\left(\cos\theta_1+i\sin\theta_1\right)\left(\cos\theta_1-i\sin\theta_1\right)}=\frac{\cos\theta_1-i\sin\theta_1}{\cos^2\theta_1+\sin^2\theta_1}=\cos\theta_1-i\sin\theta_1,
$$

since $\cos^2\theta_1+\sin^2\theta_1=1$ and $i^2=-1$. Therefore

$$
z^{-1}=\frac{1}{r_1}\left(\cos\theta_1-i\sin\theta_1\right)=\frac{1}{r_1}\operatorname{cis}\left(-\theta_1\right)=\frac{1}{r_1}\cos\theta_1-\frac{1}{r_1}i\sin\theta_1.
$$

For (2), expand the product and group the real and the imaginary parts:

$$
zw=r_1r_2\left(\cos\theta_1+i\sin\theta_1\right)\left(\cos\theta_2+i\sin\theta_2\right)=r_1r_2\left[\left(\cos\theta_1\cos\theta_2-\sin\theta_1\sin\theta_2\right)+i\left(\sin\theta_1\cos\theta_2+\cos\theta_1\sin\theta_2\right)\right],
$$

and the angle-sum identities

$$
\cos\left(\theta_1+\theta_2\right)=\cos\theta_1\cos\theta_2-\sin\theta_1\sin\theta_2,\quad \sin\left(\theta_1+\theta_2\right)=\sin\theta_1\cos\theta_2+\cos\theta_1\sin\theta_2,
$$

give $zw=r_1r_2\left(\cos\left(\theta_1+\theta_2\right)+i\sin\left(\theta_1+\theta_2\right)\right)=r_1r_2\operatorname{cis}\left(\theta_1+\theta_2\right)$.

For (3), apply (1) and (2):

$$
\frac{z}{w}=zw^{-1}=r_1\operatorname{cis}\left(\theta_1\right)\cdot\frac{1}{r_2}\operatorname{cis}\left(-\theta_2\right)=\frac{r_1}{r_2}\operatorname{cis}\left(\theta_1-\theta_2\right).
$$

For (4), repeated application of (2) gives $z^n=r_1^n\operatorname{cis}\left(n\theta_1\right)$ for every integer $n>0$, and (1) extends the identity to every integer $n<0$. If $\zeta=\rho\operatorname{cis}(\phi)$ is an $n$th root of $z$, then

$$
\rho^n\operatorname{cis}\left(n\phi\right)=r_1\operatorname{cis}\left(\theta_1\right),
$$

hence $\rho^n=r_1$ and $n\phi=\theta_1+2k\pi$ for some integer $k$. Since $\rho$ is a non-negative real number, $\rho=r_1^{\frac{1}{n}}$, and

$$
\phi=\frac{\theta_1+2k\pi}{n}.
$$

The choices $k=0,1,\dots,n-1$ give $n$ distinct arguments, hence the $n$ distinct $n$th roots of $z$; the choice $k=0$ is the root written in (4).
{{End hidden}}
